state.misconception_label: Does not understand that 2n represents an even number

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: Which of these shows part of the proof that the sum of two odd numbers is even? I got \( \begin{array}{l}2 n+(2 m+1) \\ =2(n+m)+1\end{array} \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you explain why you chose to add \(2n\) and \(2m+1\) together in that way? How does that align with the definition of even and odd numbers? Let's break down the reasoning behind your calculation to ensure we are on the right track.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I thought that since \(2n\) is just some number and \(2m+1\) is an odd number, when you add them together, you just get a new number. But now I'm confused because you said \(2n\) is even, so how does that work with the odd number? Does that mean I should have done something different?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of any examples where adding an even number to an odd number results in an even number? Let's explore why that might be the case and how it relates to the definitions of even and odd numbers that we discussed earlier.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher fails to directly address the student's core misconception that 2n represents an even number (which the student explicitly questions in Turn 2), instead asking about adding even and odd numbers which leads the student away from the original proof task and creates confusion about a different concept.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking, never directly provides answers, and in Turn 3 implicitly uses a counterexample approach by asking the student to test their reasoning with concrete cases, which aligns well with the Socratic method.
